This is an edited transcript of an interview with Margit Solberg, who coordinates the Hollis Street repair café, recorded for a community radio programme about local initiatives. The interviewer is Ben Archer.

Ben: Margit, for listeners who've never been to one, what is a repair café?

Margit: It's a free meeting place where people bring broken things and volunteers help them fix them. Toasters, lamps, trousers with a torn seam, bicycles, laptops, toys. Once a month, on the second Saturday, we take over the church hall on Hollis Street from ten until two. You sit down with a volunteer, and the important thing is that you fix it together. We're not a free repair shop. We want people to learn and to see that things can be opened.

Ben: How did it start?

Margit: The Hollis Street repair café opened in 2019. I'd read about the first repair cafés in the Netherlands and thought, we have a lot of retired engineers and tailors in this neighbourhood who are bored. I put a notice in the library, and eleven people turned up to the first planning meeting. Now we have about thirty volunteers on the list, and usually fifteen or so come each month.

Ben: What do people bring most?

Margit: Small kitchen appliances, by far. Kettles, toasters, coffee machines. Then clothes and textiles, then lamps, then electronics. Bikes come in waves; in spring we get a lot.

Ben: And how often can you actually fix things?

Margit: We keep records of every item, because we report to the national network. Over the last year, volunteers fix about 70 percent of items. Another 10 percent or so we diagnose and the person goes home knowing which part to order. The rest can't be fixed, at least not by us.

Ben: Why can't they be fixed?

Margit: Sometimes the thing is just worn out. But more and more it's design. Manufacturers make repair hard with glued batteries, special screws, plastic clips that snap when you open them. We get headphones where the battery is glued to the circuit board. We get coffee machines where the part that fails is only sold as part of a whole assembly that costs more than half the machine. And spare parts often aren't available at all after a few years.

Ben: Do you worry about safety? People bringing in mains-powered appliances?

Margit: Of course. Every electrical item gets a safety test at the end, by a volunteer who's a qualified electrician, before it goes home. We have insurance through the national network, and people sign a liability waiver when they come in, which says that we help in good faith but don't guarantee the repair. In six years we've never had an incident, and I'd like to keep it that way.

Ben: What does it cost to run?

Margit: Very little. The church gives us the hall for free. We spend maybe a few hundred a year on consumables — solder, fuses, thread, cable ties — and that comes from a donation jar and a small grant from the neighbourhood fund. Volunteers bring their own tools.

Ben: Who comes as visitors?

Margit: Everyone. Students, pensioners, young parents with broken toys. A lot of people come the first time to save money and come back because they enjoy it. Some visitors have become volunteers.

Ben: If you could change one thing, what would it be?

Margit: I'd want a right to repair law for spare parts that covers all the small appliances we see, not just the big ones. If manufacturers had to sell spare parts and publish repair manuals for, say, ten years, half of the things we turn away would be fixable. And batteries that can be replaced without a heat gun.

Ben: Thank you, Margit.

Margit: Thank you. And come along on the second Saturday — bring something broken.
key_points: Hollis Street repair café opened in 2019
volunteers fix about 70 percent of items
manufacturers make repair hard with glued batteries
insurance and liability waiver
wants a right to repair law for spare parts

title: Postmortem: 3-hour outage of the payments API
text:
Postmortem: payments API outage, 3 hours 12 minutes

Status: final. Format: blameless. Authors: platform reliability team, with input from payments engineering and customer support.

Summary

On Thursday, between 14:07 and 17:19 UTC, the payments API unavailable for 3 hours 12 minutes for most requests. During that period about 91 percent of requests to create or capture payments failed with HTTP 503 or timed out. Merchants could not take card payments through our API, and our hosted checkout page showed an error. Roughly 184,000 payment attempts failed. No payment was charged twice and no data was lost or exposed; payments that failed were not charged.

The trigger was a configuration change that lowered a database client timeout. The connection pool exhausted after a config change lowered the timeout, because slow queries that previously completed now timed out and were retried, holding connections longer overall. A retry storm from clients amplified the load. Recovery took much longer than the change itself, because the rollback was delayed: the deploy tool depended on the same database that was overloaded.

Impact

- 14:07 to 17:19 UTC: payment creation and capture success rate fell from a normal 99.95 percent to between 6 and 12 percent.
- Around 184,000 failed payment attempts across about 9,300 merchants. Many merchants' customers retried successfully after recovery; we estimate the number of payments that were lost entirely, where the customer did not return, at between 30,000 and 50,000, but we cannot measure this precisely.
- Refunds and payouts, which run on a separate service, were not affected.
- Our status page was updated 23 minutes after the start of the incident, which is too slow.

Background

The payments API runs on a fleet of about 120 application instances. Each instance holds a pool of up to 40 connections to the primary payments database through a connection proxy. The proxy limits the total number of server connections to 3,000. Under normal load, the fleet uses about 1,400 connections at peak.

Two weeks before the incident, an investigation into tail latency found that a small fraction of queries — mostly reporting queries issued by the merchant dashboard through the same API — occasionally ran for 20 to 30 seconds and tied up connections. The team decided to lower the client-side statement timeout from 30 seconds to 5 seconds so that slow queries would fail fast and release their connections.

Timeline (UTC)

- 13:58 The timeout change is merged. Configuration changes are applied to the whole fleet at once by the configuration service, which pushes new values to every instance within about a minute.
- 14:02 All instances are running with the 5-second timeout.
- 14:07 The daily settlement reconciliation job starts, as it does every day at that time. It issues heavy queries against the payments database. Database CPU rises to 85 percent, as usual for this job. Under the old timeout, some API queries slowed down but completed. Under the new timeout, a growing number of ordinary payment queries exceed 5 seconds, time out, and are retried by the application's database client, which retries twice by default. Each retry takes a new connection while the database is still working on the abandoned query.
- 14:09 Connection count at the proxy reaches its limit of 3,000. New requests wait for a connection and time out. Error rate climbs past 50 percent. Alerts fire for the error rate and the connection count.
- 14:11 The on-call engineer acknowledges the alerts and starts investigating. The settlement job is suspected first, because of its timing.
- 14:16 Merchant integrations, many of which retry failed API calls immediately and several times, triple the request rate within five minutes. This is the retry storm. Our API's own rate limiting is per merchant, and most merchants stay within their individual limits, so it does not help.
- 14:24 The settlement job is paused. Database CPU falls, but the connection pool stays exhausted, because retries and the incoming retry storm keep it full.
- 14:30 The status page is updated, 23 minutes after impact began.
- 14:41 The configuration change is identified as the likely trigger by comparing the change log with the start of the incident. The incident commander decides to roll it back.
- 14:44 The rollback through the configuration service fails. The configuration service stores its state in a schema on the same database cluster, and its own queries time out. Engineers try twice more and fail.
- 15:05 An engineer suggests changing the timeout through an environment variable override and restarting instances. This requires the deploy tool, which also reads deployment metadata from the same database cluster, and also fails.
- 15:20 The team decides to shed load at the edge: the load balancer is configured to reject 70 percent of payment traffic with a 503 and a Retry-After header, to let the database recover. The load balancer configuration is managed separately and the change succeeds.
- 15:38 Connection count falls below the limit. The configuration service becomes responsive.
- 15:46 The timeout rollback is applied through the configuration service. Instances pick up the 30-second timeout within a minute.
- 16:05 Load shedding is reduced to 40 percent. Error rates for admitted traffic are normal.
- 16:40 Load shedding is reduced to 10 percent.
- 17:19 Load shedding is removed. Success rate is back to normal. The incident is closed at 17:45 after an hour of monitoring.

Root cause and contributing factors

1. A timeout reduction applied to the whole fleet at once. The change was reviewed and was reasonable in isolation, but nobody tested it under the load of the settlement job, which runs daily and slows ordinary queries. The fleet-wide rollout meant every instance was affected at the same moment, with no canary to catch the problem.

2. Retries inside the database client multiplied the load. A query that times out after 5 seconds is not cancelled immediately on the server; the database keeps working on it until it notices the client has gone. Retrying immediately means the same expensive work runs two or three times in parallel.

3. Client retries without backoff. Many merchant integrations retry immediately, and our documentation does not say clearly enough that they should use exponential backoff with jitter. Our API does not send Retry-After headers on 503 responses from the application, only from the load balancer.

4. The recovery path shared a dependency with the failing system. The configuration service and the deploy tool both depended on the overloaded database cluster. This turned a ten-minute rollback into a 65-minute delay.

5. Slow status page updates. The process required the incident commander to approve the text, and the incident commander was busy.

What went well

- Alerts fired within two minutes of impact.
- Load shedding at the load balancer worked as intended and was the turning point of the recovery.
- No double charges: idempotency keys on payment creation prevented duplicates when merchants retried.

Customer communication

Merchants learned about the outage mainly from their own customers and from their monitoring, not from us. The status page update at 14:30 said only that we were "investigating elevated error rates", and it was not updated again until 15:40. Support received about 2,600 tickets and 400 phone calls during the incident; the phone queue reached a wait time of 50 minutes. After the incident we emailed all affected merchants with a summary, a list of their failed payment attempts with timestamps, and advice on contacting customers whose payments had failed. Several large merchants asked for service credits under their contracts, which are being handled by account management under the normal terms.

Merchants told us that the most useful thing during the incident would have been a clear statement of what was failing, what was not, and when they should expect the next update, even without an estimate of recovery time. The status page template now has fields for exactly those three things.

Action items

Action items: retry budgets, staged config rollout, and removing the shared dependency.

1. Staged config rollout: configuration changes go to 5 percent of instances first, then 25 percent, then everyone, with automatic halts if error rates rise. Owner: platform. Due: four weeks.
2. Retry budgets: the database client may spend at most 10 percent of its requests on retries over any one-minute window, and retries use backoff with jitter. Owner: payments engineering. Due: three weeks.
3. Cancel abandoned queries on the server when a client times out. Owner: database team. Due: three weeks.
4. Move the configuration service and the deploy tool's metadata off the payments database cluster. Owner: platform. Due: eight weeks.
5. Return Retry-After on application-level 503 responses and update the integration guide to require exponential backoff with jitter. Owner: developer experience. Due: two weeks.
6. Move merchant dashboard reporting queries to a read replica. Owner: payments engineering. Due: six weeks.
7. Allow the on-call engineer to post a pre-approved first status update without waiting for the incident commander. Owner: support. Due: one week.
8. Add a load test that runs the settlement job together with peak payment traffic before any change to database timeouts or pool sizes. Owner: reliability. Due: six weeks.

Lessons

A change that makes each individual request safer can make the system less safe, when it interacts with retries. Timeouts, retries and pool sizes must be changed together and tested under realistic load. And every system needs a way to recover that does not depend on the thing that is broken.
key_points: payments API unavailable for 3 hours 12 minutes
connection pool exhausted after a config change lowered the timeout
retry storm from clients amplified the load
rollback was delayed because the deploy tool depended on the same database
action items: retry budgets, staged config rollout

title: Postmortem: search index rebuild locked the orders table
text:
Postmortem: orders table locked during a schema migration

Date of incident: Monday. Duration of impact: 26 minutes. Severity: 2. Author: Ines Carvalho, on behalf of the storefront team.

What happened

At 10:14 local time, a routine deploy ran a database migration that added an index on the orders table to speed up a new customer search feature. The migration added an index without CONCURRENTLY. In Postgres, a plain CREATE INDEX takes a lock that blocks all writes to the table until the index is built. The orders table has about 140 million rows, and building the index took 26 minutes. The orders table locked for 26 minutes, from 10:14 to 10:40.

Impact

Order placement failed during the lock: every attempt to insert into the orders table waited for the lock and eventually timed out after 30 seconds. About 4,700 checkout attempts failed. Customers saw a generic error page and their payments were not taken. Order history pages kept working, because reads were not blocked. No data was lost or corrupted. Customer support received 310 contacts in the following two hours.

Detection and response

The checkout error rate alert fired at 10:16. The on-call engineer saw that the deploy had just run and that all failing queries were waiting on a lock held by the migration. The team discussed cancelling the migration, which would have released the lock immediately, but the index was already more than half built and the deploy tool marks a cancelled migration as failed, which blocks further deploys until someone fixes the migration state by hand. Under pressure, the team estimated the remaining build time at about ten minutes and decided to wait. The estimate was wrong — the build took another sixteen minutes. In hindsight, cancelling at 10:18 would have ended the impact at once, and the cost of repairing the migration state afterwards was small compared with sixteen more minutes of failed checkouts.

Why it happened

The migration was written by an engineer who usually works on a service that uses a different database and was not familiar with the CONCURRENTLY option. It passed code review because the reviewer focused on the search code and the migration was four lines long. The migration also passed the staging deploy, because the staging orders table has only 200,000 rows and the index built in under a second there. Nothing in our process checks migrations for locking behaviour or relates staging timing to production size.

What we are changing

1. A migration linter now rejects blocking index creation. It runs in CI and fails any migration that creates an index without CONCURRENTLY, adds a column with a volatile default, or changes a column type on a table that is listed as large. A migration can override the linter with an explicit comment that explains why, and the override requires approval from a database owner.
2. Migrations that touch large tables run in a separate deploy step, outside business hours, with a lock timeout of five seconds so that they fail fast instead of blocking traffic.
3. Our incident guide now says: when a migration is blocking production traffic, cancel it first and repair state afterwards. Waiting for a long-running operation to finish is not a recovery plan.
4. The staging database will be refreshed with a production-sized, anonymised copy of the orders table, so that slow migrations show up before production.

Follow-up checks

We audited the migrations merged in the last twelve months for the same pattern and found two more that created indexes on large tables without CONCURRENTLY. Both had run at night, when traffic was low enough that nobody noticed the lock. Neither caused an alert, which means our alerting would not have caught this class of problem outside peak hours either.

We thank the support team, who handled a large number of customer contacts with very little notice.
key_points: migration added an index without CONCURRENTLY
orders table locked for 26 minutes
order placement failed during the lock
migration linter now rejects blocking index creation

title: How to rotate an SSH key without locking yourself out
text:
SSH keys should be rotated when someone leaves a team, when a laptop is lost, or simply on a schedule. The risk in rotation is locking yourself out of a server by removing the old key before the new one works. This guide avoids that by keeping both keys valid until the new one is proven.

1. Generate a new key. On your own machine, generate a new ed25519 key: ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your-name rotated-2026-10". Use a passphrase. Ed25519 keys are short, fast and supported by every reasonably recent OpenSSH server. Save it under a new filename, such as ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_2026, so that the old key stays in place for now.

2. Add the new public key. Copy the new public key to each server with ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_2026.pub user@server. This appends it to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys. The important rule: add the new public key to authorized_keys before removing the old one. At this point both keys work.

3. Test in a second session. Keep your current SSH session open. In a second terminal, connect with only the new key: ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_2026 -o IdentitiesOnly=yes user@server. IdentitiesOnly stops your SSH agent from quietly offering the old key, which would make the test meaningless. If the login fails, you still have the first session to fix things.

4. Update everything else that uses the key: your ~/.ssh/config entries, deployment tools, Git hosting accounts and any CI secrets.

5. Remove the old key. Once the new key works everywhere, remove the old key from every server by deleting its line from authorized_keys. The line ends with the comment you gave the old key, which is why meaningful comments matter. Then test again with the new key, in a new session.

6. Retire the old private key: delete it from your machine and from your SSH agent with ssh-add -d.

If you manage many servers, do this with your configuration management tool rather than by hand, and keep a list of which servers you have rotated so that none keeps the old key forever.
key_points: generate a new ed25519 key
add the new public key to authorized_keys before removing the old one
test the new key in a second session
remove the old key from every server

title: Setting up encrypted off-site backups for a small office with restic
text:
This guide shows how to set up encrypted, automated, off-site backups for a small office file server using restic. It assumes a Linux server that holds the shared folders, about 200 GB of data, and an account with any provider that offers S3-compatible object storage. Allow two hours for the initial setup and a few hours for the first upload, depending on your connection.

Why restic

restic is a free, open-source backup program. It encrypts everything on your machine before upload, so the storage provider cannot read your files. It deduplicates data, so a nightly backup only uploads what changed, and keeping a year of daily snapshots costs little more than one full copy. It works with many storage back ends; here, restic backs up to an S3-compatible bucket.

A backup that lives in the same building as the server does not protect you against fire, theft or ransomware that encrypts every drive it can reach. Off-site, encrypted, versioned backups do. A sync service that mirrors the shared folders to the cloud is not a substitute either: when a file is deleted or encrypted on the server, the sync service faithfully deletes or encrypts the copy too. A backup needs history, so that you can go back to the state before the mistake or the attack.

Step 1: create the bucket and credentials

In your storage provider's console, create a new bucket, for example office-backups. Enable object versioning if the provider offers it; it adds protection if an attacker gains access to the backup credentials and tries to delete data. Create an access key that can only read and write this one bucket. Do not use your account's main credentials.

Step 2: install restic

On Debian or Ubuntu: sudo apt install restic. Then run sudo restic self-update to get the latest version, since distribution packages can be old. Check with restic version.

Step 3: create a configuration file

Create /etc/restic/env, readable only by root (chmod 600), containing:

export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=your-access-key
export AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=your-secret-key
export RESTIC_REPOSITORY=s3:https://s3.your-provider.example/office-backups
export RESTIC_PASSWORD_FILE=/etc/restic/password

Then create /etc/restic/password, also chmod 600, containing a long random password. You can generate one with openssl rand -base64 32.

Step 4: store the repository password safely

This is the step people skip and regret. Without the repository password, your backups are unreadable — by you as well as by attackers. There is no recovery. If the server burns down, the password file burns with it. Store the repository password in a password manager that at least two people in the office can access, and keep a printed copy in a sealed envelope somewhere outside the office, such as with the owner at home or in a safe deposit box. Do the same with the storage access keys, or at least with the login to the storage provider's console.

Step 5: initialise the repository

source /etc/restic/env && restic init

restic creates the repository structure in the bucket and encrypts it with your password.

Step 6: run the first backup

source /etc/restic/env && restic backup /srv/shared --exclude-caches --exclude '*.tmp'

The first backup uploads everything and can take many hours on a typical office connection: 200 GB at 50 megabits per second of upload is roughly nine hours. Run it in the evening or over a weekend, inside a tmux or screen session so that it survives you logging out. Later backups only upload changes and usually take minutes.

If the server hosts databases or accounting software with open files, do not back up their live files directly; a copy taken while the program is writing can be corrupt. Use the program's own export or dump function first, write the dump to a folder, and back up that folder.

Step 7: schedule nightly backups with a systemd timer

Create /etc/systemd/system/restic-backup.service:

[Unit]
Description=restic backup
[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/bin/bash -c 'source /etc/restic/env && restic backup /srv/shared --exclude-caches && restic forget --keep-daily 14 --keep-weekly 8 --keep-monthly 12 --prune'

And /etc/systemd/system/restic-backup.timer:

[Unit]
Description=nightly restic backup
[Timer]
OnCalendar=*-*-* 01:30:00
Persistent=true
[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target

Enable it with sudo systemctl enable --now restic-backup.timer. Persistent=true means a backup missed because the server was off will run at the next boot. You can schedule nightly backups with cron instead, but a systemd timer gives you logs in the journal (journalctl -u restic-backup) and handles missed runs.

Step 8: retention with restic forget --prune

Without a retention policy, snapshots accumulate forever. The command in the service above keeps the last 14 daily snapshots, the last 8 weekly snapshots and the last 12 monthly snapshots, and then prunes data that no snapshot references any more. That gives you a year of history, which is enough to recover a file someone deleted months ago without noticing. Adjust the numbers to your needs. Pruning can take a while on large repositories; if it makes the nightly job too slow, move the forget --prune part into a separate weekly timer.

Step 9: get told when backups fail

A backup that silently stopped working three months ago is the most common way small offices lose data. Add a notification. The simplest option is a health-check service: create a check that expects a ping every day, and add a curl call to its URL at the end of the ExecStart command, so it pings only when the backup succeeded. If no ping arrives, the service emails you. Alternatively, have systemd send an email on failure with an OnFailure= unit.

Also run restic check once a week. It verifies the repository's structure. Once a month, run restic check --read-data-subset=5% to download and verify a sample of the actual data.

Step 10: test restores every month

A backup you have never restored is a hope, not a backup. Test restores every month, and write the date and result in a log that someone else in the office can see. To list snapshots: restic snapshots. To restore one folder from the latest snapshot to a temporary location:

restic restore latest --target /tmp/restore-test --include /srv/shared/finance

Open a few of the restored files and check that they are complete. Once a year, do a full disaster-recovery test: on a spare machine or a cloud server, with nothing but the printed password and the storage credentials from the envelope, install restic and restore everything. This tests your documentation as much as your backups. The first time most offices do this, they discover something missing — usually the password.

Protecting backups from ransomware

Ransomware increasingly looks for backups and deletes them before encrypting the main data, because a victim with good backups does not pay. If an attacker takes over the file server, they also have the credentials in /etc/restic/env. Three measures help.

First, the bucket versioning from step 1 means that deleted or overwritten objects can still be recovered from the provider's console for a period you choose, often 30 days. Some providers also offer object lock, which prevents deletion of objects for a fixed period even with valid credentials; if yours does, enable it for at least two weeks.

Second, you can run the backups through a restic REST server in append-only mode, on a separate small machine or a cloud server that the office file server cannot log in to. In append-only mode, the file server can add new snapshots but cannot delete old ones. Pruning then runs on the REST server itself, on its own schedule, with its own credentials.

Third, keep a second, offline copy of the most important data. Once a quarter, copy the repository to an external drive with restic copy and store the drive away from the office. An external drive that is unplugged cannot be encrypted by malware.

Documenting the setup

Write a one-page document that describes where the backups go, where the password and credentials are kept, how to run a restore, and who is responsible for the monthly test. Store it next to the printed password, and keep a copy in the password manager. The person who set up the backups will not always be available when a restore is needed, and in a crisis nobody wants to read restic's manual from the beginning. Update the document whenever something changes, such as a new bucket, a new storage provider or a new folder on the server.

Costs

At typical object storage prices, 200 GB of deduplicated data with a year of history costs a few dollars a month. Downloading data for a full restore can incur egress fees at some providers; check your provider's pricing so that a restore after a disaster does not come with a surprise bill.

Common mistakes

- Keeping the only copy of the repository password on the server being backed up.
- Using storage credentials that can delete the whole bucket, with no versioning, so that ransomware on the server can destroy the backups too.
- Backing up open database files instead of dumps.
- Never testing a restore.
- Forgetting that laptops are not backed up by this setup. If people keep important files only on their laptops, either sync those folders to the server or run restic on the laptops too, with a separate repository or at least a separate host name.

With an afternoon of work and a monthly ten-minute restore test, a small office can have backups that survive the loss of the whole building.
key_points: restic backs up to an S3-compatible bucket
store the repository password in a password manager
schedule nightly backups with a systemd timer
retention with restic forget --prune
test restores every month

title: Afternoon naps and next-day recall in older adults: a randomised trial
text:
Abstract

Background: Observational studies have linked daytime napping in older adults with both better and worse cognitive outcomes, but they cannot separate the effect of napping from the health conditions that make people nap. We tested whether a short, scheduled afternoon nap improves next-day memory in healthy older adults.

Methods: In a randomised trial of 214 adults aged 65 to 80 without diagnosed cognitive impairment, participants were assigned to one of three groups for four weeks: a scheduled 30-minute afternoon nap opportunity, a scheduled 90-minute nap opportunity, or a quiet-rest control in which participants read or listened to the radio while seated upright for 30 minutes. Night-time sleep measured with wrist actigraphy throughout the study. The primary outcome was delayed recall on a 20-item word-list test, administered at baseline and after four weeks by assessors who did not know the group assignment.

Results: Compared with the control group, the 30-minute afternoon nap improved word-list recall by 1.2 words (95 percent confidence interval 0.3 to 2.1) after four weeks. The 90-minute group did not differ from control (0.2 words, interval −0.8 to 1.2). Actual nap duration in the 90-minute group averaged 71 minutes; in an exploratory analysis, naps longer than 60 minutes showed no benefit and were associated with 18 minutes less night-time sleep on average. No serious adverse events occurred.

Conclusions: A short scheduled nap produced a modest improvement in next-day recall. The effect was small and needs replication in more diverse populations and over longer periods.

1. Introduction

About a quarter of adults over 65 report napping on most days. Whether this is good or bad for cognition remains contested. Large cohort studies have found that frequent or long daytime naps predict later cognitive decline, but napping is also a symptom of poor night-time sleep, depression, cardiovascular disease and early neurodegenerative change. These conditions could explain the association without napping itself causing any harm.

Laboratory studies in young adults point the other way. A short nap after learning can improve memory consolidation, apparently because stage 2 sleep and sleep spindles support the transfer of new memories into longer-term storage. Whether this applies to older adults is unclear: older people have fewer spindles and lighter sleep, and naps may also borrow sleep from the following night.

Only a few randomised studies have tested napping in older adults, and most were small (fewer than 40 participants), lasted a single day, or did not measure night-time sleep. A trial that controls nap duration, measures sleep objectively at night, and follows participants for several weeks is needed to separate the potential benefit of a short nap from the possible costs of long ones.

We designed this trial with two nap lengths because the observational literature suggests a dose-response pattern: short naps appear harmless or helpful, long naps harmful. Testing both in one trial lets us examine whether duration, rather than napping as such, matters. The quiet-rest control group sat upright to make sleep unlikely while matching the time participants spent away from other activities, and the social contact with study staff.

The trial took place in two cities, with participants recruited through general practices, community centres and newspaper advertisements. We excluded people who worked night shifts, used sleep medication, had untreated sleep apnoea, or already napped for more than an hour on most days, because a scheduled nap would change their routine less than it would change other participants'. Participants napped at home, in their own beds, and reported the start and end of each nap in a diary; actigraphy allowed us to check those reports.

Our hypotheses were that the 30-minute nap would improve delayed recall compared with control, and that the 90-minute nap would not improve recall and would reduce night-time sleep. Both hypotheses and the analysis plan were registered before recruitment began.
key_points: randomised trial of 214 adults aged 65 to 80
30-minute afternoon nap improved word-list recall
naps longer than 60 minutes showed no benefit
night-time sleep measured with wrist actigraphy
the effect was small and needs replication

title: Retrieval helps small models less than expected on multi-hop questions
text:
Abstract

Retrieval-augmented generation is widely used to give smaller language models access to knowledge they lack. We study retrieval-augmented generation with models from 1 to 13 billion parameters on questions that need one, two or three reasoning steps over retrieved documents. We introduce a new benchmark called HopTrace, with 6,200 questions whose supporting passages are annotated step by step, so that failures can be attributed to retrieval, to reading, or to combining facts. Across eight open models, retrieval improves single-hop accuracy but much less on multi-hop questions: with perfect retrieval, single-hop accuracy rises by 31 to 44 points over the closed-book baseline, but three-hop accuracy rises by only 6 to 15 points. Our step-level annotations show that the main failure is not retrieval. Even when every needed passage is in the context, small models ignore retrieved passages that contradict their prior beliefs in 27 to 41 percent of cases, falling back on what they memorised during pre-training. Simple query decomposition recovers part of the gap, raising three-hop accuracy by 9 points on average, at about three times the inference cost. We release HopTrace and our evaluation code.

1. Introduction

Large language models store a surprising amount of factual knowledge in their parameters, but this knowledge is incomplete, goes out of date, and is hard to inspect. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) addresses these problems by retrieving relevant documents at inference time and placing them in the model's context. The approach is especially attractive for smaller models, which are cheap enough to run on modest hardware and can be deployed where data must stay on premises, but which memorise less during training.

A common assumption in practice is that retrieval can close much of the gap between small and large models: if the facts are in the context, a smaller model only has to read them. For simple factual questions this is largely true. Prior work has shown that retrieval lifts small models' accuracy on single-fact questions to near the level of much larger closed-book models.

Many real questions, however, need several steps. "Which university did the founder of the company that makes the drug X attend?" needs three facts — the drug's manufacturer, the manufacturer's founder, the founder's university — and the model must combine them in order. Each step adds an opportunity for failure: the retriever may miss a passage, the model may misread one, or it may fail to connect them.

Existing multi-hop benchmarks report only final-answer accuracy, which makes it difficult to tell which of these failures dominates. A model that answers wrongly might have lacked the second passage, or might have had every passage and still produced its memorised answer. These two failures call for different remedies: better retrieval in the first case, better reading or training in the second.

1.1 Contributions

We make three contributions.

First, we introduce HopTrace, a benchmark of 6,200 questions requiring one, two or three hops, built from a snapshot of an open encyclopedia. For each question we annotate the gold passage for each step and the intermediate answer that the step should produce. About a third of the questions are counterfactual: we edit the supporting passages so that the correct answer, given the documents, differs from the real-world fact the model is likely to have memorised. Counterfactual questions let us measure whether a model reads the context or relies on its prior.

Second, we evaluate eight open models ranging from 1 to 13 billion parameters, from four model families, under three retrieval conditions: closed-book (no retrieval), realistic retrieval with a dense retriever returning the top ten passages, and oracle retrieval in which exactly the gold passages are provided along with eight distractors. Oracle retrieval removes retrieval errors entirely, so any remaining failure is a failure of reading or reasoning.

Third, we use the step annotations to attribute errors. For each failed question, we check whether the gold passages were retrieved, whether the model's output contains the correct intermediate answers when prompted to show its steps, and whether the final answer matches the counterfactual document or the memorised real-world fact.

1.2 Summary of findings

Retrieval helps multi-hop questions far less than single-hop ones. With oracle retrieval, single-hop accuracy rises by 31 to 44 points over closed-book across models. Two-hop accuracy rises by 14 to 26 points, and three-hop accuracy by only 6 to 15 points. With realistic retrieval the gains are smaller still, because the probability of retrieving every needed passage falls with each hop: our retriever finds all gold passages for 88 percent of single-hop questions but only 52 percent of three-hop questions.

Reading, not retrieval, is the larger problem for small models. Under oracle retrieval, where every needed passage is present, most errors on three-hop questions occur at the second or third step, and a large share involve the model ignoring a passage. On counterfactual questions, small models ignore retrieved passages that contradict their prior in 27 to 41 percent of cases and answer with the memorised fact instead. The rate falls with model size: the 13-billion-parameter models ignore the context least often, but even they do so in more than a quarter of counterfactual cases.

Distractors matter more than context length. Adding more distractor passages hurts multi-hop accuracy much more than single-hop accuracy, and passages that mention the same entities as the gold passage are the most harmful. Simply increasing context length with irrelevant padding has little effect.

Query decomposition helps but is expensive. Prompting the model to break the question into sub-questions, retrieving and answering each in turn, raises three-hop accuracy by 9 points on average under realistic retrieval. It also triples the number of model calls and retrieval operations, and errors in early sub-answers propagate to later steps. Query decomposition recovers part of the gap, but not most of it.

1.3 Implications

For practitioners, our results suggest caution in assuming that retrieval makes a small model adequate for complex questions. If a deployment's questions are mostly single facts, retrieval with a small model works well. If they require combining facts, a larger model or a pipeline that decomposes questions is likely to be needed, and evaluation should include questions where the documents contradict common knowledge, since these reveal whether the model actually reads its context.

For researchers, the gap between oracle and realistic retrieval, and the remaining gap between oracle retrieval and perfect accuracy, point to two separate research problems. Better multi-step retrievers address the first. The second — teaching small models to prefer evidence in the context over their memorised beliefs — may require changes to training rather than to prompting. We find that instruction-tuned variants ignore context somewhat less often than their base models, which suggests that training data emphasising grounded answers can help.

1.4 Limitations

HopTrace is built from one encyclopedia and covers questions about people, organisations, places and works. Questions about numbers, dates and comparisons are under-represented, and multi-hop reasoning in technical domains such as medicine or law may behave differently. Our counterfactual edits are designed to be plausible, but a model might reasonably distrust a document that contradicts widely known facts; in some applications, that distrust is desirable. We treat following the document as correct because the documents define the task, but we note that the right behaviour in deployment depends on how trustworthy the retrieved sources are. Finally, we evaluate models up to 13 billion parameters; we do not know whether the patterns hold for much larger models, though prior work suggests that context-following improves with scale.

1.5 Paper outline

Section 2 reviews related work on retrieval-augmented generation, multi-hop question answering and knowledge conflicts between context and parameters. Section 3 describes how HopTrace was constructed, including the annotation process, quality control and the procedure for counterfactual edits. Section 4 describes the models, retrievers and prompts. Section 5 reports results under the three retrieval conditions, and Section 6 presents the error attribution analysis. Section 7 evaluates query decomposition and two other mitigation strategies: reranking retrieved passages and instructing the model explicitly to prefer the documents. Section 8 concludes.

2. Related work (excerpt)

Multi-hop question answering has a long history of benchmarks built from linked encyclopedia articles. Most report exact-match or F1 scores on final answers. Several studies have noted that models can answer some multi-hop questions through shortcuts, for example by matching the question's wording to a single passage, without performing every step. Our step annotations allow us to detect such shortcuts: a correct final answer with an incorrect intermediate answer suggests the model did not follow the intended reasoning path. We find that shortcut answers account for about 8 percent of correct two-hop answers in the closed-book setting and under 3 percent with oracle retrieval.

Work on knowledge conflicts has shown that language models sometimes prefer their parametric knowledge over contradicting context, and that this tendency varies with model size, training and how familiar the fact is. Our counterfactual questions extend this line of work to multi-step settings, where a single ignored passage breaks the chain of reasoning even if every other step is followed correctly. We find that conflicts at the final step are resolved in favour of the context more often than conflicts at an intermediate step, possibly because intermediate facts are less salient in the prompt.

title: Postmortem: status page went down with the service it reports on
text:
Postmortem: status page unavailable during the API incident

Summary. During last Tuesday's API outage, which lasted 52 minutes, our public status page was also unavailable for the first 40 minutes. The status page hosted on the same cluster as the API, behind the same load balancer, so when the load balancer failed both went down together. Customers could not see incident updates for 40 minutes, and many concluded that we were unaware of the outage. Support received about 900 messages in that window, most asking whether we knew.

What happened. The API outage itself, caused by a faulty load balancer configuration, is covered in its own postmortem. This document covers only the status page. We built the status page in-house three years ago as a small web application. To save effort, it was deployed to the main production cluster. Nobody had written down that this meant it shared failure modes with the services it reports on, and it had never been tested during a real cluster-level outage.

At 09:12, the incident commander tried to post an update and got an error. The team then spent several minutes confirming that the status page was down for the same reason as the API, and another twenty minutes discussing whether to fix it or post updates elsewhere. At 09:52, once the load balancer was fixed, the status page came back and the first update was posted, saying the incident was already resolved.

What we changed.
1. The status page moved to an external provider that runs on separate infrastructure, in a different hosting company, with its own domain. It was migrated this week. It can be updated through a web form, so it does not depend on any of our internal tools.
2. Incident updates also posted to the support Twitter account and to an email list that customers can subscribe to, so there is more than one channel.
3. A quarterly drill: we will simulate a total outage of our own infrastructure and confirm that the on-call engineer can still publish a status update within ten minutes.
4. The incident runbook now lists "post first status update" as step two, after acknowledging the alert, with a pre-written template.
key_points: status page hosted on the same cluster as the API
customers could not see incident updates for 40 minutes
status page moved to an external provider
incident updates also posted to the support Twitter account
